Switch Attention: Towards Dynamic and Fine-grained Hybrid Transformers

Yusheng Zhao Email: zhangmeng92@huawei.com    Hourun Li Email: yinyichun@huawei.com    Bohan Wu Email: Shang.Lifeng@huawei.com    Jingyang Yuan    Meng Zhang    Yichun Yin Affiliation:  Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.    Lifeng Shang Affiliation:  Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.    Ming Zhang Affiliation:  State Key Laboratory for Multimedia Information Processing, School of Computer SciencePKU-Anker LLM Lab, Peking University Affiliation:  Contribution during internship at Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.{yusheng.zhao,lihourun}@stu.pku.edu.cn, {wxtpku,yuanjy,mzhang_cs}@pku.edu.cn
Abstract

The attention mechanism has been the core component in modern transformer architectures. However, the computation of standard full attention scales quadratically with the sequence length, serving as a major bottleneck in long-context language modeling. Sliding window attention restricts the context length for better efficiency at the cost of narrower receptive fields. While existing efforts attempt to take the benefits from both sides by building hybrid models, they often resort to static, heuristically designed alternating patterns that limit efficient allocation of computation in various scenarios. In this paper, we propose Switch Attention (SwiAttn), a novel hybrid transformer that enables dynamic and fine-grained routing between full attention and sliding window attention. For each token at each transformer layer, SwiAttn dynamically routes the computation to either a full-attention branch for global information aggregation or a sliding-window branch for efficient local pattern matching. An adaptive regularization objective is designed to encourage the model towards efficiency. Moreover, we adopt continual pretraining to optimize the model, transferring the full attention architecture to the hybrid one. Extensive experiments are conducted on twenty-three benchmark datasets across both regular (4K) and long (32K) context lengths, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method.

1 Introduction

The transformer architectures Vaswani et al. (2017); Dai et al. (2019); Kitaev et al. (2020) have been widely adopted in recent large language models (LLMs) Anil et al. (2023); OpenAI (2023); Singh et al. (2025). Despite their success in language modeling, standard transformer architectures suffer from quadratic computational complexity due to the attention mechanism Vaswani et al. (2017). To address this limitation, efforts have been made in reducing the compuation of standard full attention Shazeer (2019); Dao et al. (2022); Ainslie et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2024a), sparsifying full attention Child et al. (2019); Kitaev et al. (2020); Liu et al. (2022a); Zhang et al. (2023); Xiao et al. (2023); Song et al. (2024); Xu et al. (2025); Yuan et al. (2025), developing sub-quadratic attention mechanisms Katharopoulos et al. (2020); Ma et al. (2021); Han et al. (2023); Peng et al. (2023a); Yang et al. (2024); Gu and Dao (2024); Peng et al. (2025); Guo et al. (2025a), and designing hybrid transformer models Beltagy et al. (2020); Zaheer et al. (2020); Jiang et al. (2023); Fu et al. (2024); Du et al. (2025).

Among these solutions, hybrid transformer models leverage both standard full attention and its efficient variants, e.g., sliding window attention (SWA, Beltagy et al. 2020), and have been widely adopted in larger industrial models Gemma (2024); Yang et al. (2025); OpenAI (2025); Gao et al. (2026). While they balance efficiency and performance of language modeling, most hybrid transformers adopt a static hybrid scheme (e.g., alternating between full attention and sliding window attention with a fixed ratio) designed heuristically prior to the pretraining stage Brown et al. (2020); Jiang et al. (2023); Singh et al. (2025); Du et al. (2025). This limits the model’s potential to allocate computation more efficiently. For example, when the context beyond the range of a sliding window is less relevant to the response that the model is about to generate, one would expect a lower ratio of expensive standard full attention, and vice versa.

Towards this end, this paper proposes a novel hybrid attention mechanism named Switch Attention (SwiAttn). As is shown in Figure 1, the proposed SwiAttn is a dynamic and fine-grained hybrid solution compared to prior efforts. In particular, SwiAttn inserts a router before each attention module and dynamically decides whether the input feature should be processed by standard full attention or sliding window attention for each token at each transformer layer. The full attention branch gathers long-range information accurately from the entire sequence, while the sliding window branch models short-term memory efficiently from a narrower context. The router dynamically decides the specific branch for each token at each layer based on the input feature. In order to encourage the router towards the more efficient branch (i.e., the SWA branch), we adopt a regularization objective that is optimized with the log-likelihood loss. Additionally, to efficiently transfer the knowledge from pretrained full attention models, we utilize continual pretraining (CPT, Sun et al. 2020; Mendieta et al. 2023; Yıldız et al. 2024; Guo et al. 2025b) to convert the standard full attention architecture to the proposed SwiAttn. We perform extensive experiments on twenty-three benchmark datasets covering different context lengths against several competing baselines, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of SwiAttn. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

  • ❶

    New Perspective: We present a dynamic and fine-grained perspective of hybrid transformer models for effective allocation of computation between full attention and its efficient variants.

  • ❷

    Novel Methodology: We propose Switch Attention (SwiAttn), consisting of both the full attention branch and the SWA branch, to adaptively allocate computation for each token’s representation at each transformer layer. Additionally, we design an adaptive regularization objective and optimize the model from standard transformers through continual pretraining.

  • ❸

    Empirical Validation: We conduct extensive experiments on twenty-three benchmark datasets covering commonsense reasoning, in-context retrieval, and long-context understanding. Further experiments reveal the dynamics of the routing, enabling fine-grained allocation of computation.

2 Related Works

2.1 Efficient Attention Mechanism

The quadratic computational complexity has become a major bottleneck of efficient transformer-based LLMs as input sequences grow longer. This leads to a plethora of efforts in designing efficient attention mechanisms Tay et al. (2022); Sun et al. (2025). One line of research attempts to reduce the computation of the standard full attention itself by sharing Shazeer (2019); Ainslie et al. (2023) and compressing Ge et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2024a); Liu et al. (2024b); Liu et al. (2024c) the key and value vectors, or optimizing hardware compatibility Dao et al. (2022); Chang et al. (2025); Sanovar et al. (2025). Another line of work designs mechanisms to sparsify the standard full attention through heuristic Zaheer et al. (2020); Xiao et al. (2023) or data-dependent patterns Xu et al. (2025); Nawrot et al. (2025); Lai et al. (2025); Yuan et al. (2025). To circumvent the quadratic complexity, efforts are made in employing sub-quadratic attention Yang et al. (2024); Han et al. (2024); Dao and Gu (2024); Peng et al. (2025); Guo et al. (2025a); Kimi et al. (2025). However, their efficiency comes at the expense of degraded long-context performance, as their memory is limited by the size of the state matrices Guo et al. (2025a); Nazari and Rusch (2026); Sun et al. (2026). Conceivably, efficiency often comes at a price, and different mechanisms might be suitable for distinct scenarios, motivating the design of hybrid transformer models.

2.2 Hybrid Transformers

Hybrid transformer models have been widely adopted to enhance the efficiency of LLMs Jiang et al. (2023); Gemma (2024); Yang et al. (2025). Most hybrid transformers consists of both standard full attention and its efficient variants, such as sliding window Child et al. (2019), sparse Zaheer et al. (2020), or linear attention Yang et al. (2024); Kimi et al. (2025). A common practice among existing designs is to interleave full and efficient attention layers (e.g., Figure 1(a)) according to a static ratio empirically defined before training Wang et al. (2025); OpenAI (2025); Xiao et al. (2026). Given the heuristic nature of these methods, efforts are made in automated search for optimal hybrid configurations under certain data distributions Gu et al. (2025); Acun et al. (2025); Xia et al. (2026). Nevertheless, most existing approaches adhere to a static hybrid scheme, either heuristically defined Kitaev et al. (2020); Kimi et al. (2025); Yang et al. (2025) or searched with data Gu et al. (2025); Liu and Wang (2025), while recent works suggest distinct difficulty in generating tokens Leviathan et al. (2023); Cai et al. (2024); Gloeckle et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2024a); Fu et al. (2025). Therefore, this work proposes a dynamic and fine-grained hybrid transformer to efficiently allocate computation across tokens and transformer layers.

3 Methodology

3.1 Preliminaries and Framework Overview

Preliminaries and Notations. We consider the standard language modeling task. During the pretraining stage, the input sentence is first tokenized and then transformed to the hidden representations 𝑯(1)=[𝒉1(1),𝒉2(1),…,𝒉T(1)]∈ℝd×T\bm{H}^{(1)}=[\bm{h}_{1}^{(1)},\bm{h}_{2}^{(1)},...,\bm{h}_{T}^{(1)}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times T}, where TT is the sequence length and dd is the hidden dimension size. At the ll-th transformer layer, the input hidden representations 𝑯(l)\bm{H}^{(l)} is mapped into queries, keys and values through a linear mapping ϕ\phi, i.e., [𝑸(l),𝑲(l),𝑽(l)]=ϕ⁡(𝑯(l))[\bm{Q}^{(l)},\bm{K}^{(l)},\bm{V}^{(l)}]=\phi(\bm{H}^{(l)}). Attention (standard full attention or a more efficient one) is computed using 𝑸(l),𝑲(l),𝑽(l)\bm{Q}^{(l)},\bm{K}^{(l)},\bm{V}^{(l)} to obtain the attended output 𝑶(l)\bm{O}^{(l)}. Finally, a feed-forward network is applied to obtain the input hidden representations (i.e., 𝑯(l+1)\bm{H}^{(l+1)}) of the next transformer layer. The final hidden representation 𝑯(L+1)\bm{H}^{(L+1)} (where LL is the number of transformer layers) is used to predict the next token. During the decoding stage, the model generates one token each time with the current query 𝒒t(l)\bm{q}_{t}^{(l)}, key 𝒌t(l)\bm{k}_{t}^{(l)} and value 𝒗t(l)\bm{v}_{t}^{(l)}, and uses KV cache {𝒌i(l),𝒗i(l)}i=1t−1\{\bm{k}_{i}^{(l)},\bm{v}_{i}^{(l)}\}_{i=1}^{t-1} to store previously computed key and value vectors. 11 1 For simplicity, we omit some details here and in the following, such as layer normalization, residual connection, position embeddings, attention heads, etc.

Framework Overview. The proposed SwiAttn is a dynamic and fine-grained hybrid of standard full attention and SWA, as illustrated in Figure 2. At each transformer layer during the continual pretraining stage, both full attention and SWA are computed using the shared queries, keys and values. A router is applied to the input hidden representations to decide which branch to use for each token. The attended outputs from the two branches are then gathered and processed by a feed-forward layer. An adaptive regularization objective is applied to the output of each router to encourage the model towards the SWA branch. During the decoding stage, the router is first applied to the hidden representation to decide the branch for computing, and the model only computes the selected branch using a shared KV cache.

3.2 Dual-branch Routing

The proposed SwiAttn consists of two branches: the full attention branch and the SWA branch. Standard full attention excels in capturing long-range dependencies, while SWA efficiently computes attended output using local contexts. Not all tokens require global information at all transformer layers: there is a natural sparsity in both layer Yang et al. (2025); Kimi et al. (2025); Gao et al. (2026) and token Leviathan et al. (2023); Cai et al. (2024); Fu et al. (2024); Fu et al. (2025) dimensions. Therefore, we use a router function to decide the specific branch to use.

Concretely, given the input hidden representation 𝑯(l)∈ℝd×T\bm{H}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times T} at the ll-th layer, we first compute the soft gate using the router function ℛ\mathcal{R} as:

σ~(l)=sigmoid⁡(ℛ⁡(𝑯(l)))∈[0,1]T,\tilde{\sigma}^{(l)}=\operatorname{sigmoid}\left(\mathcal{R}(\bm{H}^{(l)})\right)\in[0,1]^{T}, (1)

where sigmoid⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sigmoid}(\cdot) is the sigmoid function. The (hard) gate indicating the path of computation for each token at the ll-th layer, σ(l)∈{0,1}T\sigma^{(l)}\in\{0,1\}^{T}, is then obtained by applying a threshold τ=0.5\tau=0.5, i.e.,

σ(l)=𝟙​(σ~(l)>τ)+σ~(l)−sg⁡(σ~(l)),\sigma^{(l)}=\mathds{1}\left(\tilde{\sigma}^{(l)}>\tau\right)+\tilde{\sigma}^{(l)}-\operatorname{sg}\left(\tilde{\sigma}^{(l)}\right), (2)

where 𝟙​(⋅)\mathds{1}(\cdot) is an element-wise indicator function and sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) is the stop gradient function. Note that we adopt straight-through estimation (STE, Fedus et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2022b; Huh et al. 2023) to enable differentiation of the router’s parameters during training. The gate is used to control whether a corresponding token should be computed with full (when the value is 11) or sliding window attention (when the value is 00). Subsequently, we compute both the full attention branch and the SWA branch using a shared set of queries, keys and values, i.e.,

[𝑸(l),𝑲(l),𝑽(l)]=ϕ⁡(𝑯(l)),\displaystyle[\bm{Q}^{(l)},\bm{K}^{(l)},\bm{V}^{(l)}]=\phi(\bm{H}^{(l)}), (3)
𝑶FULL(l)=𝒜FULL(l)​(𝑸(l),𝑲(l),𝑽(l)),\displaystyle\bm{O}_{\text{FULL}}^{(l)}=\mathcal{A}_{\text{FULL}}^{(l)}(\bm{Q}^{(l)},\bm{K}^{(l)},\bm{V}^{(l)}), (4)
𝑶SWA(l)=𝒜SWA(l)​(𝑸(l),𝑲(l),𝑽(l)),\displaystyle\bm{O}_{\text{SWA}}^{(l)}=\mathcal{A}_{\text{SWA}}^{(l)}(\bm{Q}^{(l)},\bm{K}^{(l)},\bm{V}^{(l)}), (5)

where 𝒜FULL(l)\mathcal{A}_{\text{FULL}}^{(l)} and 𝒜SWA(l)\mathcal{A}_{\text{SWA}}^{(l)} denote full attention and SWA, respectively. The gate is then used to select the output of attention 𝑶(l)\bm{O}^{(l)}, i.e.,

𝑶(l)=σ(l)⊙𝑶FULL(l)+(1−σ(l))⊙𝑶SWA(l),\bm{O}^{(l)}=\sigma^{(l)}\odot\bm{O}_{\text{FULL}}^{(l)}+(1-\sigma^{(l)})\odot\bm{O}_{\text{SWA}}^{(l)}, (6)

where ⊙\odot denotes element-wise product (in the sequence length dimension). Finally, the feed-forward network (FFN) is applied to obtain the hidden representation at the (l+1)(l+1)-th layer.

During inference, the attention output is computed similarly. At the prefill stage, the attention output can be computed via Eq.1-6, and especially, the computation of the two branches could be further merged with a hardware-efficient implementation. At the decode stage, we compute the (hard) gate for the tt-th token at the ll-th layer as a scaler σt(l)∈{0,1}\sigma^{(l)}_{t}\in\{0,1\}, and then compute the full attention or SWA accordingly. Notably, in the decoding stage, both branches share a single set of KV-cache to increase inference efficiency. We summarize the inference procedure of SwiAttn in Algorithm 1.

3.3 Adaptive Regularization

In the dual-branch routing framework, the full attention branch provides richer information than the SWA branch. Therefore, to encourage the model towards the SWA branch for efficiency, we also design an adaptive regularization objective that is optimized during continual pretraining. Conceivably, when the ground-truth token exhibits lower log-likelihood under the predicted distribution, the model may struggle to predict this token, and therefore, we expect higher ratios for the more powerful full attention branch. Additionally, when the two branches disagree, we also tend toward the more reliable full attention branch. These require the regularization objective to be more adaptive.

Specifically, given the soft gate of the tt-th token at the ll-th transformer layer σ~t(l)\tilde{\sigma}_{t}^{(l)}, the regularization objective is designed as follows:

ℒt(l)=γt(l)​sp⁡(ℛ⁡(𝒉t(l))),\mathcal{L}_{t}^{(l)}=\gamma_{t}^{(l)}\operatorname{sp}\left(\mathcal{R}(\bm{h}_{t}^{(l)})\right), (7)

where γt(l)\gamma_{t}^{(l)} is the adaptive weight of regularization discussed in the following, and sp⁡(x)=ln⁡(1+ex)\operatorname{sp}(x)=\ln(1+e^{x}) is the softplus function, a smooth version of the ReLU function Nair and Hinton (2010), providing a small penalty to values less than 00 and increasing penalty to values greater than 00. The adaptive weight γt(l)\gamma_{t}^{(l)} of the tt-th token at the ll-th layer is determined by several factors: (1) the base weight γbase\gamma_{\text{base}}, (2) the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the ground-truth token under the currently predicted distribution of language modeling, i.e., NLL⁡(t)\operatorname{NLL}(t), and (3) the disagreement of the two branches as measured by the mean squared error (MSE), i.e., ∥𝒐FULL(t,l)−𝒐SWA(t,l)∥22\lVert\bm{o}_{\text{FULL}}^{(t,l)}-\bm{o}_{\text{SWA}}^{(t,l)}\rVert^{2}_{2}, where 𝒐FULL(t,l)\bm{o}_{\text{FULL}}^{(t,l)} and 𝒐SWA(t,l)\bm{o}_{\text{SWA}}^{(t,l)} denotes the output of the full attention branch and the SWA branch of the tt-th token at the ll-th layer. Considering these factors, the adaptive weight γt(l)\gamma_{t}^{(l)} can be written as follows:

γt(l)=γbaseε+NLL⁡(t)+α⋅∥𝒐FULL(t,l)−𝒐SWA(t,l)∥22,\gamma_{t}^{(l)}=\frac{\gamma_{\text{base}}}{\varepsilon+\operatorname{NLL}(t)+\alpha\cdot\lVert\bm{o}_{\text{FULL}}^{(t,l)}-\bm{o}_{\text{SWA}}^{(t,l)}\rVert^{2}_{2}}, (8)

where ε\varepsilon and α\alpha are hyper-parameters.

Remark. Eq.8 adaptively reweight the regularization objective of the router. The hyperparameter ε\varepsilon avoids division by zero and provides an upper bound of the weight, i.e., γt(l)≤γbase⋅ε−1\gamma_{t}^{(l)}\leq\gamma_{\text{base}}\cdot\varepsilon^{-1}. The NLL and MSE terms reduce the weight of regularization when the token prediction loss increases (high NLL) and/or the two branches diverge (high MSE). Under such conditions, the reduced regularization weights encourage the router to use fewer SWA branches and more full attention branches, since the SWA branch may be less reliable.

3.4 Continual Pretraining

Different from many hybrid transformers that require training from scratch, the proposed SwiAttn adopts a continual pretraining approach, utilizing the learned knowledge from an existing off-the-shelf full attention transformer.

In particular, given a standard transformer and its full attention module at the ll-th layer 𝒜~FULL(l)\tilde{\mathcal{A}}_{\text{FULL}}^{(l)}, we initialize parameters of both the full attention branch 𝒜FULL(l){\mathcal{A}}_{\text{FULL}}^{(l)} and the SWA branch 𝒜SWA(l){\mathcal{A}}_{\text{SWA}}^{(l)} of SwiAttn using the parameters of 𝒜~FULL(l)\tilde{\mathcal{A}}_{\text{FULL}}^{(l)}. Other parameters like the FFN layer are also inherited from the standard pretrained transformer. During the continual pretraining stage, we train the entire hybrid transformer using both the language modeling objective ℒLM\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}} and the aforementioned adaptive regularization objective, i.e.,

ℒ=ℒLM+1L​T​∑l=1L∑t=1Tℒt(l).\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}+\frac{1}{LT}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathcal{L}_{t}^{(l)}. (9)

By continual pretraining from an existing standard transformer, we save computation resources and stabilize the optimization process. The CPT process of SwiAttn is presented in Algorithm 2.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setups

Datasets. Three types of datasets are used. ▶\blacktriangleright Commonsense Reasoning, including Lambada (LMB., Paperno et al. 2016), Wikitext (Wiki., Merity et al. 2016), BoolQ Clark et al. (2019), PIQA Bisk et al. (2020), SIQA Sap et al. (2019), HellaSwag (Hella., Zellers et al. 2019), WinoGrande (Wino., Sakaguchi et al. 2021), ARC-easy and ARC-challenge (ARC-e and ARC-c, Clark et al. 2018), and OpenBookQA (OBQA, Mihaylov et al. 2018); ▶\blacktriangleright In-Context Retrieval from Arora et al. 2024, including SWDE Lockard et al. (2019), FDA Arora et al. (2023), TriviaQA (TQA, Joshi et al. 2017), NQ Kwiatkowski et al. (2019), DROP Dua et al. (2019), and SQuAD (SQD, Rajpurkar et al. 2018); ▶\blacktriangleright Long-Context Understanding from LongBench-E Bai et al. (2024), including MultiFieldQA (MFQA, Bai et al. 2024), TRec Li and Roth (2002), MultiNews (MNs, Fabbri et al. 2019), GovReport (GvR, Huang et al. 2021), Qasper (Qas, Dasigi et al. 2021), TriviaQA (TQA, Joshi et al. 2017), and SAMSum (SSM, Gliwa et al. 2019). Since we are experimenting with a 1.51.5B model, we only include datasets that yield reasonable scores. More details can be found in Appendix A.

Baselines. We compare the proposed SwiAttn against several baselines, including sliding window attention (both zero-shot and continual pretraining versions, marked as SWA-ZS and SWA-CPT), the static hybrid of full attention and SWA commonly used in larger industrial LLMs Brown et al. (2020); OpenAI (2025); Xiao et al. (2026) (with ratio of 1:3, marked as StaticHybrid), and full attention (marked as FullAttn). More details about baseline implementation can be found in Appendix B.

Implementation Details. For the transformer architecture, we use a 1.51.5B language model with 2222 transformer layers (i.e., L=22L=22). Each layer contains a dual-branch routing module and an FFN layer. The router function ℛ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{R}(\cdot) is implemented with a linear mapping, and the threshold τ\tau is set to 0.50.5. For the SWA branch, the window size is set to 10241024. In adaptive regularization, we set the base weight γbase\gamma_{\text{base}} to 1×10−31\times 10^{-3}, the ε\varepsilon to 0.10.1 and the weight α\alpha to 100100. For model optimization, we first pretrain the 1.51.5B full attention model on 44K-length sequences using 240240B tokens and then continually pretrain the SwiAttn model for 2020B tokens. To evaluate tasks of longer sequences, we optimize the 3232K full attention model by pretraining on 44K context lengths for 192192B tokens and then extending the context length using YaRN Peng et al. (2023b) to 3232K with 2424B tokens. The corresponding SwiAttn is obtained by continual pretraining on the full attention model for another 88B tokens. More details can be found in Appendix C.

4.2 Main Results

We compare the performance of SwiAttn against baselines on 2828 benchmark datasets, and the results are shown in Table 1, Table 2 and Table 3.

Commonsense Reasoning. We present the results on commonsense reasoning datasets in Table 1. As the contexts of most instances are within the sliding window size (i.e., 10241024), the performance of SwiAttn is similar to the baselines, including both full attention and SWA models.

In-Context Retrieval. The results on in-context retrieval datasets are presented in Table 2. For these datasets, most contexts are within the 40964096 token limit of 44K-length models, and some instances require attention spans longer than the sliding window size. The results show that full attention and hybrid models (including SwiAttn) outperform SWA baselines by a large margin on average. Additionally, the proposed SwiAttn achieves a relative improvement of 27.5%\bm{27.5\%} compared to SWA-CPT and 4.5%\bm{4.5\%} compared to StaticHybrid, reaching the same average score as FullAttn.

Long-Context Understanding. The results on long-context understanding datasets are shown in Table 3. For these datasets, the contexts of most instances grows beyond the 10241024 window size and can be as long as the maximum context of 3232K, which requires strong long-context capability of the models. As can be seen from the results, SwiAttn achieves the best average performance among the baseline methods, surpassing all baselines on average. Particularly, SwiAttn achieves a relative improvement of 6.3%\bm{6.3\%} compared to the StaticHybrid baseline, despite using full attention less frequently (as we will show in Section 4.4).

4.3 Ablation Studies

To investigate the effect of different mechanisms in the proposed method, we design several variants of the original SwiAttn. Specifically, V1 disables adaptive regularization and uses γbase\gamma_{\text{base}} instead. V2 removes the NLL term in Eq.8. V3, V4, and V5 changes α\alpha from 100100 to 1010, 11, and 00, respectively. V6 and V7 perturb ε\varepsilon from 0.10.1 to 0.20.2 and 0.010.01. We present results on three summarization datasets from LongBench-E in Table 4.

Effect of Adaptive Regularization. From V1, V2, and V5, we can see that adaptive regularization, along with several factors in adaptive weights, is effective. The removal of adaptive regularization reduces average performance by 1.31.3. Besides, when the NLL (V2) or MSE (V5) terms are removed, the performance also declines.

Effects of Hyperparameters. V3 and V4 show the effect of the hyperparameter of α\alpha. When α\alpha is changed, the accuracy drops, as α\alpha balances the relative importance of the MSE term in adaptive regularization. Variants V6 and V7 show the effect of ε\varepsilon. The model is less sensitive to this hyperparameter, and when ε\varepsilon is perturbed, the accuracy decreases slightly. ε\varepsilon controls the upper bound of the adaptive weights, which affects the optimization process.

4.4 Further Analysis

Needle-in-a-Haystack. We also provide experimental results on the commonly-used Needle-In-A-Haystack (NIAH) task using RULER Hsieh et al. (2024). Specifically, we test 3535 different context positions (i.e., depth percent) and 3535 context lengths (i.e., token limit). The retrieval tests are repeated three times for each case, and the results are visualized in Figure 3. As can be seen from the results, the proposed SwiAttn achieves perfect retrieval accuracy across various scenarios, showing that SwiAttn maintains the strong retrieval capability of full attention with its dynamic routing mechanism models under long context lengths.

Inference Efficiency. We compare the inference efficiency of SwiAttn and the FullAttn baseline. For the prefill stage, we plot the amount of computation required (in terms of GFLOPs) at every token position, following Liu et al. 2025, and the results are shown in Figure 4(a). For the decode stage, we measure efficiency with the amount of memory access of the KV cache (in terms of the number of tokens at each layer on average), as it is the primary bottleneck of the decoding speed of attention. As the efficiency of SwiAttn is related to the data distribution, we provide results on both standard (under the same distribution of training corpus) and simple (under the distribution of needle-in-a-haystack task where the needle is within the sliding window) setups in Figure 5(a). As can be seen from the results, the proposed SwiAttn achieves over 𝟒×\bm{4\times} speedup at 3232K context lengths under standard data distribution and as much as 𝟏𝟐×\bm{12\times} speedup for decoding under simple data distributions.

Ratios of Full Attention across Layers. We then investigate how different transformer layers behave in dual-branch routing. Specifically, we collect the routing decisions of each transformer layer and calculate the ratio of the model choosing full attention under the 3232K continual pretraining data distribution and count the decisions of 400400M tokens. The results are presented in Figure 5. As can be seen from the results, different transformer layers exhibit distinct patterns of routing: some layers (e.g., Layer 1, 2, 3, 22) tend to use more SWA branches while others (e.g., Layer 8, 11, 14) use full attention branches more frequently. This suggests different layers specialize in different functionalities. Additionally, we also compute the averaged full attention ratio of all layers, and the result is around 0.130.13, which is lower than the 0.250.25 ratio of conventional static hybrid models with one full attention layer after three SWA layers.

Dynamics in Dual-Branch Routing. We also investigate the dynamics of dual-branch routing. When the next token can be easily predicted based on information within the sliding window, we expect the model to use the SWA branch more frequently, and when the next token is hard to forecast with local information, the full attention branch should be more frequently used as a default choice. To verify whether SwiAttn behaves in a computation efficient way, we resort to the NIAH retrieval task, where needles to be retrieved are inserted in different locations of the context (i.e., different depth percent, higher percents indicate closer distance to the end of the prompt), and measure the full attention ratio of SwiAttn when generating the answer (i.e., the inserted needle). The results are presented in Figure 6, where we illustrate the ratio under different context lengths (i.e., 1.91.9K, 2.82.8K, 3.73.7K, 4.64.6K, 30.230.2K). The results show that when the needle is inserted in lower depth percentages (outside the sliding window), the model chooses around 3030% of full attention, while when the model is closer to the end of the prompt (within the sliding window), a lower ratio of full attention around 55% is observed. This demonstrates that SwiAttn can dynamically and efficiently decide the specific branch to use based on the context.

5 Conclusion

This paper presents Switch Attention (SwiAttn), a novel hybrid transformer that can dynamically route the hidden representation to either full attention or sliding window attention at each transformer layer, enabling efficient and fine-grained allocation of computation based on the contexts. SwiAttn can be optimized via continual pretraining from off-the-shelf standard full attention transformers. An adaptive regularization objective is designed to enhance efficiency while maintaining accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed SwiAttn, and further empirical results reveal its dynamics and efficiency.

Limitations

One limitation of this work is the lack of a hardware-efficient implementation for computing the two branches during the prefill stage. Another limitation is that we have not verified the effectiveness of the method on larger models beyond 1.51.5B parameters due to limited computational resources. In the future, we plan to develop hardware-efficient kernels and verify the method on larger models.

Appendix A Details about the Datasets

In this section, we provide comprehensive descriptions of the datasets used in our experiments, organized by the three evaluation categories: commonsense reasoning, in-context retrieval, and long-context understanding.

A.1 Commonsense Reasoning

This category evaluates models’ ability to perform reasoning based on everyday world knowledge.

  • •

    Lambada (LMB.) (Paperno et al., 2016): A word prediction task requiring broad discourse context understanding. Models must predict the final word of a passage, which cannot be inferred from local context alone. The dataset contains 5,153 test passages extracted from BookCorpus. We report perplexity on the standard test set.

  • •

    Wikitext (Wiki.) (Merity et al., 2016): A language modeling dataset derived from Wikipedia articles. We evaluate perplexity on the test split to assess generative capability over coherent, long-form text.

  • •

    BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019): A binary question answering dataset where questions are naturally occurring yes/no queries from Google search. Evaluation is based on exact match accuracy.

  • •

    PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020): Physical Interaction QA, focusing on everyday physical reasoning. Models choose between two plausible solutions to a goal. Accuracy is reported on the test set.

  • •

    SIQA (Sap et al., 2019): Social Interaction QA, assessing understanding of social commonsense. Models select the most appropriate response to a given situation among candidates.

  • •

    HellaSwag (Hella.) (Zellers et al., 2019): A challenging dataset for commonsense natural language inference (NLI), requiring models to predict the most plausible continuation of an event description among four candidates. Normalized accuracy is evaluated on the test split.

  • •

    WinoGrande (Wino.) (Sakaguchi et al., 2021): A large-scale Winograd schema dataset with 44K problems designed to test pronoun disambiguation with adversarial filtering. Binary accuracy is reported.

  • •

    ARC-easy & ARC-challenge (ARC-e/c) (Clark et al., 2018): The AI2 Reasoning Challenge, containing grade-school science questions. ARC-e consists of relatively straightforward questions, while ARC-c includes more challenging ones requiring multi-step reasoning. Accuracy is reported for ARC-e while normalized accuracy is reported for ARC-c.

  • •

    OpenBookQA (OBQA) (Mihaylov et al., 2018): A dataset requiring external commonsense knowledge beyond the provided “open book” fact. Models answer multiple-choice science questions; evaluation is based on normalized accuracy.

A.2 In-Context Retrieval

Following Arora et al. (2024), this category assesses models’ ability to retrieve and utilize relevant information from a maximum of 4,0964,096 token context. We employ Cloze Completion Formatting prompts to align with next-word-prediction training objectives.

  • •

    SWDE (Lockard et al., 2019): A structured extraction dataset where models answer questions by retrieving attribute values from semi-structured web pages (HTML).

  • •

    FDA (Arora et al., 2023): Food and Drug Administration document QA, requiring extraction of specific regulatory information from PDF documents.

  • •

    TriviaQA (TQA) (Joshi et al., 2017): A large-scale reading comprehension dataset with question-answer-evidence triples.

  • •

    Natural Questions (NQ) (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019): Real user queries to Google Search with answers annotated on Wikipedia pages.

  • •

    DROP (Dua et al., 2019): A dataset requiring discrete reasoning over numerical and temporal information. Models generate answers via span extraction, counting, or arithmetic.

  • •

    SQuAD (SQD) (Rajpurkar et al., 2018): Stanford Question Answering Dataset, where answers are text spans from Wikipedia passages.

A.3 Long-Context Understanding

We adopt benchmark datasets from LongBench-E (Bai et al., 2024) to evaluate performance on tasks requiring processing of extended contexts. The benchmark is constructed from the following sources.

  • •

    MultiFieldQA (MFQA) (Bai et al., 2024): MFQA is a multi-domain QA dataset with long documents spanning legal, scientific, judicial, and government fields. Answers require synthesizing information across distant passages.

  • •

    TRec (Li and Roth, 2002): TRec is a question classification task requiring models to categorize questions into 50 predefined topic classes.

  • •

    MultiNews (MNs) (Fabbri et al., 2019): MultiNews is a multi-document summarization dataset containing news articles about the same event.

  • •

    GovReport (GvR) (Huang et al., 2021): GovReport is a long-document summarization task based on U.S. government reports and congressional hearings.

  • •

    Qasper (Qas) (Dasigi et al., 2021): Qasper is a QA dataset over NLP research papers, featuring questions requiring understanding of methodology, results, and claims.

  • •

    TriviaQA (TQA) (Joshi et al., 2017): The TriviaQA dataset in LongBench-E is is a long-context variant of the original version, where relevant evidence is embedded within extended passages to test retrieval under length pressure.

  • •

    SAMSum (SSM) (Gliwa et al., 2019): The SAMSum dataset consists of messenger-like conversations as the input with summaries annotated by human as the target.

A.4 Evaluation Metrics

We adopt different evaluation metrics for these datasets. Specifically, for Lambada and Wikitext, we use perplexity. For BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, WinoGrande, and ARC-e, we use accuracy. For HellaSwag, ARC-c, and OpenBookQA, we use normalized accuracy. For in-context retrieval tasks, we use the “contains" metric and follow the prompt template of Arora et al. 2024. For LongBench-E, we use the default evaluation metric provided in Bai et al. 2024 with implementation from Gao et al. 2024.

Appendix B Details about the Baselines

In this part, we provide more details about the implementation of the baseline models.

  • •

    SWA-ZS. The zero-shot sliding window attention baseline is implemented using the corresponding full attention model. It directly restricts the attention span of full attention transformers to 10241024 in alignment with SwiAttn.

  • •

    SWA-CPT. The continually pretrained sliding window attention model is obtained by performing CPT on the SWA-ZS model. We use the same amount of tokens as the proposed SwiAttn to train this baseline model.

  • •

    StaticHybrid. The StaticHybrid baseline is implemented by alternating full attention layers and SWA layers. Specifically, we adopt the ratio of 1:3, where one full attention transformer layer is placed after three SWA transformer layers. In the 2222-layer transformer model, the 4,8,12,16,204,8,12,16,20-th layers are implemented with full attention, while the remaining layers are implemented with sliding window attention. The StaticHybrid baseline is initialized using the pretrained full attention model and continually pretrained under the same token budget as SwiAttn for a fair comparison.

  • •

    FullAttn. The full attention baseline is a 1.51.5B language model with 2222 transformer layers. The hidden size is set to 20482048. The standard version is trained on 240240B tokens of 44K context lengths, while the 3232K version is trained on 192192B tokens of 44K lengths and 2424B tokens of 3232K lengths.

Appendix C Additional Implementation Details

In the experiments, we adopt a 1.51.5B transformer model with 2222 layers and the hidden dimension of 20482048. For the attention module, group query attention Ainslie et al. (2023) is used with 1616 attention heads and 88 key-value heads. The dimension of each query, key, and value vectors is set to 128128. In dual-branch routing, the router function ℛ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{R}(\cdot) is applied after the root-mean-square (RMS) layer normalization Zhang and Sennrich (2019).

For the 44K-length model, we first pretrain the full attention transformers with 240240B tokens, where we set the batch size to 10241024 and train for 6000060000 steps. During the first 20002000 steps of the pretraining, we linearly warmup the learning rate from 00 to 1×10−31\times 10^{-3}. During the last 1200012000 steps, we decay the learning rate to 00 with a cosine schedule. For the continual pretraining of SwiAttn, we first initialize the model as described in Section 3.4 and then continually pretrain the model for another 2020B tokens with the same batch size for 50005000 steps. During the CPT stage, we linearly warm up the learning rate from 00 to 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} for 500500 steps and decay the learning rate in the remaining 45004500 steps with a cosine schedule.

For the 3232K-length version of the model, we first pretrain the full attention transformer model for 192192B tokens on 44K-length text, and then extend the context length to 3232K using YaRN Peng et al. (2023b). Then we train the full attention model on 3232K-length texts for another 2424B tokens with the batch size of 128128 for 60006000 steps. During the first 20002000 steps, the learning rate linearly warms up to 1×10−31\times 10^{-3}, and during the last 2424B token on the 3232K-length texts (i.e., last 60006000 steps), the learning rate is decayed to 00 under a cosine schedule. The 3232K-length version of SwiAttn is first initialized using the aforementioned full attention model as described in Section 3.4 and then continually pretrained for another 88B tokens with the same batch size (i.e., 128128) for another 20002000 steps. In the first 200200 steps, we warm up the learning rate from 00 to 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, and in the remaining 18001800 steps, we decay the learning rate to 00 using a cosine schedule.

We use Megatron-LM Shoeybi et al. (2019) to train the transformer model and adopt LM-Eval-Harness Gao et al. (2024) to evaluate the models on various datasets. For the NIAH experiments, the RULER Hsieh et al. (2024) setup is applied. All experiments are performed on Ascend 910C NPUs.

Appendix D Loss Curves

In this part, we provide the loss curves of model optimization. Specifically, we visualize the language modeling loss of (a) pretraining of the full attention transformer on 44K-length sequences; (b) continual pretraining of SwiAttn on 44K-length sequences; (c) pretraining of the full attention transformer on 3232K-length sequences; (d) continual pretraining of SwiAttn on 3232K-length sequences. The results are presented in Figure 7. These curves suggest that the optimization procedure of SwiAttn is relatively stable with no loss spikes. Additionally, the continual pretraining stage of SwiAttn optimization is also stable, showing that CPT can be used as a reliable approach to convert standard full attention models to the proposed SwiAttn architecture.

Appendix E Changes of Full Attention Ratio during Continual Pretraining

In this part, we present the changes of the full attention ratios during the continual pretraining stage. Specifically, we measure the frequency of the router choosing the full attention branch during CPT on the pretraining data. The averaged ratio of full attention is presented in Figure 9, while the averaged full attention ratio of each layer is visualized in Figure 8 (where the curves are smoothed for better visualization). From the results, we can see that the proposed SwiAttn chooses the full attention branch with a frequency of around 0.130.13, which is more efficient compared to common static hybrid methods that alternate between full attention and SWA with a ratio of 1:3 (i.e., around 0.250.25 full attention ratio). Moreover, the per-layer statistics of SwiAttn suggests that different layers exhibit distinct behaviors: some layers (e.g., Layer 8, 11, 13, 14) tend to use full attention more frequently, whereas others (e.g., Layer 1, 2, 3, 22) tend to use SWA more frequently. Moreover, these results shows that the changes of full attention ratio is relatively smooth, and that the ratio stablizes after around 500500 iterations.
